seo.title: Karmic tail 21 7 4 compatibility: The World, The Chariot, The Emperor
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 7 4 compatibility: a couple who want the whole world, live on the road and must learn to rule a kingdom of two by counsel, not by decree.

title: 21-7-4 in compatibility: the whole world, a ship and a kingdom for two
short: 21-7-4 in a compatibility reading is the couple's karmic tail: The World at the entry, The Chariot in the middle, The Emperor as the main task. Such a couple starts with a dream the size of the whole world, lives it out on roads, in moves and separations, and learns to build a kingdom for two — a home, money and decisions ruled by counsel rather than decree. This triple never occurs in a personal destiny matrix: it can only come from two dates.

sections.h2: How the 21-7-4 tail is formed and why a personal matrix never has it
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple's tail works the same way: entry is added to entry, middle to middle, main task to main task. The middle is not recalculated separately — it is a sum just like the other two points.
An example: the dates 05.12.1975 and 09.05.1976. The first partner has the personal tail 18-3-12 and centre 6, the second has the tail 3-22-19 and centre 11.
The couple's centre in this example is 6 + 11 = 17, The Star; the couple's values are 6, The Lovers.

There is no other way to 21-7-4. Going through every date gives one single pair of personal tails: **18-3-12 and 3-22-19, in a hundred per cent of such couples**. This shows what the three cards are made of. The couple's World is The Moon plus The Empress (18 + 3). The Chariot is The Empress plus The Fool (3 + 22). The Emperor is The Hanged Man plus The Sun (12 + 19). Personal tails are read by their own rules, and their meaning cannot be carried over to the couple; but the arithmetic says one thing: The Empress sits in both partners' tails, and The Emperor in neither. The ruler of this union is born only in the sum. And the tale this page turns to next opens with "If I were the tsaritsa" said three times, and the tsar in it steps out from behind a fence.

Why no single person has this tail: in a personal matrix the entry of the tail M equals the main task D plus the centre. For the entry to be 21 when D = 4, the centre would have to be 17 — and 17 never stands at the centre of a personal matrix, for any date. In the couple the same equation holds exactly: **4 + 17 = 21**, The Emperor plus The Star give The World. That is why The Star stands at the centre of every such couple, without exception.

The tail is rare: about one couple in 537 (0.186%), 75th of the 97 couple tails. There are no couple tails made of the same numbers in another order. The first number of a couple's tail is always divisible by three, so 4-7-21 and 7-21-4 are impossible for a couple, and the calculation never gives 21-4-7 for any dates. If 21, 7 and 4 stand in a row in a destiny matrix, it is compatibility, and they should be read as a task for two.

sections.h2: "If I were the tsaritsa": entry to the task — The World
paragraphs: "The Tale of Tsar Saltan" begins with three wishes spoken aloud late one evening. The first sister would "prepare a feast for the whole christened world", the second "alone would weave linen for the whole world", the third would "bear a bogatyr" — a hero — for the tsar. (Quotations from Pushkin here are our own close translation.) All this time the tsar stood "behind the fence", and "the last one's speech pleased him most of all". He married her that same evening.

These lines hold a detail that appears only next to the source. In 1824 Pushkin wrote down a folk version of the tale, most likely from his nanny, and there the eldest sister boasted that she would "feed the state with a single grain". Pushkin replaced the state with "the whole world", and the word for world, mir, occurs in the tale exactly twice — in these two wishes. After that the world is called svet, and the merchants measure it: "We have sailed round the whole world" is heard eight times. The state did not vanish from the tale. It moved to the end, to the island of Buyan. The tale runs the same way as the tail: from the whole world to a kingdom of one's own.

The entry to the task is the couple's common language and shared wishes. For a 21-7-4 couple this language is wide. Early dates are about countries rather than flats: a year in another country, a house by the sea, a business of their own, friends from all over the world around one table. Lisovskaya describes The World in a couple through freedom, travel, a shared outlook, moves and even a marriage across nationalities. The two recognise each other by their scale.

But the entry point stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. The three sisters have three different "whole worlds": one wants a feast for everyone, another work for the whole world, the third a family. In a couple it is the same. One means guests and celebration by "the whole world", another a venture that will make a name, a third children and a line. Each is sure the dream is shared, until they have to decide what to spend a Saturday, money and ten years of life on. In the minus of The World, Lisovskaya has no agreements, each pulling the blanket their own way, re-educating the partner into one's own outlook, and mocking the partner's plans.

The card has a second side too. Six days after his wedding, on 24 February 1831, Pushkin wrote to Pletnyov: "I am married — and happy; my one wish is that nothing in my life should change — I shall wait for nothing better." He finished the tale that same summer at Tsarskoye Selo: a scrap of the manuscript is dated 29 August 1831. In Waite's divinatory list for The World, "voyage" and "change of place" stand side by side, and reversed comes "permanence". A 21-7-4 couple wants both at once: the whole world — and for everything to stay forever as it was on the first evening.

sections.h2: A ship, a barrel and a bumblebee: middle of the task — The Chariot
paragraphs: The Chariot enters the tale right after the wedding night: "In those days there was a war." The tsar mounts "his good steed" and rides away. From then on everything in the tale rides and sails. The barrel with the tsaritsa and her son rocks on the ocean, ships pass Buyan to the refrain "The wind roams over the sea and drives the little ship along", and the prince flies after a ship three times — as a mosquito, a fly and a bumblebee. Rimsky-Korsakov's famous "Flight of the Bumblebee" comes from the opera based on this tale (1900): it is the music to which Gvidon, as a bumblebee, flies after the ship.

The middle of the task is how the couple travels from the shared wish to the main task. For a 21-7-4 couple that road is motion. Such couples often get on best on the move: they pack a flat overnight, find a home and work in a strange city within a week, become a team on a trip. Lisovskaya writes that a Chariot couple looks from outside more like friends and a team than like lovers: each develops outside the home, decisions come fast, and they defend their own at once. That is how the Swan is saved in the tale. The young prince breaks off an oak bough, strings it with the silk cord from his cross, shoots — and the kite falls into the sea.

Wen notes something important about The Chariot: it is "travel not for the sake of travel, but for the sake of acquisition". The merchants in the tale trade in sables, horses and damask steel. Gvidon first asks "to get a wondrous wonder", then: "I would like to bring a marvellous marvel into my domain." A 21-7-4 couple is always acquiring something too: a new city, a new post, the next project. The Chariot can also sting. Lisovskaya names aggression first among The Chariot's tasks, and every flight of Gvidon's ends in a sting: one aunt in the right eye, the other in the left eye, the old woman on the nose.

But the tale's real disaster happens not at war but on the road between two people. When the tsar hears of the "unknown little beast", he first wants in his anger to hang the messenger, then softens and acts wisely: he orders them "to wait for the tsar's return for a lawful decision". On the way the messenger is made drunk, the letter is swapped, and the boyars read aloud a decree that is no longer his. In the language of a couple: one is away, the other at home, and everything important travels through go-betweens. A voice message heard in a taxi. News "Mum passed on". A row in a chat where each answers not the words but the tone they read into them. A decision taken while the other was not there, and announced aloud by somebody else.

In the minus, Lisovskaya's Chariot means hasty conclusions, conflicts out of nothing, rivalry over who leads, and a habit of drawing strength from those close rather than restoring it oneself. Among the couple's tasks she also names this one: to dare a joint move. In the tale the move is forced — in a tarred barrel. They get out of it not because someone unlocks it. The son braces his head against the bottom and says, "How could we cut a window out to the yard?" — and "knocked out the bottom and walked out".

sections.h2: The city on Buyan: main task — The Emperor
paragraphs: The morning after the Swan is saved, a city stands on the empty island: crenellated walls, golden domes, a harbour "with a strong customs post". The court meets the young prince "in golden carriages", and at once "crowns him with a prince's cap". The Chariot and The Emperor in two neighbouring lines: the carriages roll up — and the crown goes on.

Then Pushkin describes in detail how the kingdom works. For the squirrel that cracks golden nuts the prince builds a crystal house, sets a guard on her "and made a clerk keep strict account of the nuts. Profit to the prince, honour to the squirrel." Coins are cast from the shells, emeralds are poured into the storerooms, "everyone on that island is rich, there are no huts, only palaces everywhere". The thirty-three bogatyrs are "all equal, as if hand-picked" and patrol the city. The Pushkin scholar Sergei Bondi believed that the image of an ideal sea-kingdom was brought into the folk tale by Pushkin himself. The result is almost word for word Waite's divinatory list for The Emperor: "Stability, power, protection, realization".

The couple's main task is read mostly through the minus: what does not work and what to learn. For The Emperor, Lisovskaya names a struggle for leadership, decisions made for everyone, rigid rules that later get in their own makers' way, and a coldness that makes it impossible to tell joy from anger. The tale has a portrait of this minus. Three times in a row, word for word: "Tsar Saltan sits in his hall, on the throne and in his crown, with a sad thought on his face." Around him sit the weaver, the cook and the matchmaker Babarikha, who "look him in the eyes". The tsar does not say what saddens him. The tsar does not go himself. Three times he promises, "I will visit the wondrous island", — and stays. He learns about the world from other people's stories, and each time his wish to visit the wondrous island is put out by the story of a bigger wonder — "you won't surprise us with that", as the weaver says. In the folk note of 1824 the tsar is called "Sultan Sultanovich, the Turkish sovereign", and the Arabic word sultan means "power". Power sits on the throne — and sees through other people's eyes.

In a couple this looks ordinary. The rule "I keep the budget" was set when one earned and the other studied, and kept long after it all turned the other way round. "Holidays at my parents'" was decided in the first year and never revisited. One sits silent and sad on a throne, the other rules by reports and by the look on a face. And both are sure the house is in order.

The tale's own words divide it into two kingdoms. In the first half, "order", "letter" and "decree" rule — five times in twenty-four lines, and all of it by messenger. At the end the same matters are settled by "counsel": the Swan says "I will serve you with counsel", and the mother blesses the young pair "to live in counsel and love". The word for order survives on the island too, but now it serves the wonder: a chancery clerk — in Russian a d'yak prikaznyi, literally a "clerk of orders" — counts the nuts. The Emperor does not have to disappear. He has to stop writing decrees through go-betweens.

Gvidon gets the squirrel and the bogatyrs the same way: he longs, asks and receives. The third "marvel" begins with the same formula: "Grief and longing eat at me: people marry; I look around — only I go unwed." And here the Swan stops him for the first time: "But a wife is no mitten: you can't shake her off your white hand, nor tuck her into your belt… Think it all through well, so as not to repent later." A squirrel can be put under guard, a coin can be sent around the world. A person cannot be acquired, tucked into a belt or kept under guard. For the couple's Emperor this is the main lesson: **a partner is not a mitten, not a treasury and not a subject**. In the tale, sex hands out the roles. In a 21-7-4 couple either of the two can turn out to be the tsar, the messenger or the Swan, and usually both take turns.

The Emperor grows up in the tale in a single line. Hearing for the fourth time about the wonders of Buyan, Saltan stops listening to the aunts: "What am I — a tsar or a child? — he says, not joking. — I'm going today!" In Waite's reversed list for The Emperor the last word is "immaturity". The child-tsar learns about the world from stories at court. The grown tsar boards a ship and sees for himself. And at the end the truth is revealed without words: Gvidon leads his father into the city "saying nothing", and "the tsar looks — and recognises".

sections.h2: A star on her brow: a centre that belongs to neither partner
paragraphs: The star on the brow appears in the tale five times, and Babarikha is the first to mention it: "By day she outshines God's light, by night she lights the earth, the moon gleams beneath her braid, and on her brow a star burns." In the folk note these marks belonged to another hero. There the tsaritsa gives birth to a wonderful boy: "a star on his brow, a moon at the nape". The star on the brow was the child's — the one born of two. Pushkin gave it to the bride.

The same happens to the centre of a 21-7-4 couple. The centre is the couple's atmosphere, what is between two people when nobody is watching. Here it is The Star for everyone without exception, and it is a card no person ever has at the centre. These two have no "my" Star and "your" Star. It appears only between them. Lisovskaya writes about The Star at the centre of a couple with striking precision: such people often understand only in the couple who they want to be, and open up, sometimes with the partner's direct help.

That is exactly what happens in the tale. Four times the Swan finds the prince on the shore and asks the same thing: "Why are you quiet as a rainy day? What makes you sad?" Four times he confesses his longing, and she helps: three times she splashes him with water so that he can fly after the ship, she gives him the squirrel, sends her brothers the bogatyrs, and the fourth time she reveals who she is. Waite writes that the figure on The Star "pours Water of Life", and that the card's mottoes are "Waters of Life freely" and "Gifts of the Spirit". Wen sees in The Star the generosity of "giving more than the Seeker receives", and an inner compass: "Guidance is not coming from others, but rather it is coming from within."

Stars first appear in the tale above the barrel: "Stars sparkle in the blue sky, waves lash in the blue sea." Waite's divinatory list for The Star opens with "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment" and only then says "another reading says — hope and bright prospects". The night scene holds both readings: mother and child are cast into the sea, but the stars are above them, and the wave carries the barrel ashore.

There is one more coincidence that is hard to miss, though it proves nothing. The Swan's portrait is made of three lights: the moon, a star, and a radiance that outshines the day. In the Major Arcana these three cards come in a row: 17 — The Star, 18 — The Moon, 19 — The Sun. In a 21-7-4 couple The Moon stands in one partner's personal tail, The Sun in the other's, and The Star at the centre of their shared matrix. Pushkin, of course, knew nothing of the matrix.

Lisovskaya's minus of The Star is love for an image instead of a person, comparison with others, fitting the partner to a picture. Gvidon falls in love with a rumour: he hears about the princess from Babarikha while sitting as a bumblebee at his father's court, and doubts it himself: "But come — is it true?" The answer comes not from rumour but from the one who has been beside him the whole tale: "Why go far? Know that your fate is near: that princess is me." This is the turn of the whole tail. The World at the entry and The Chariot in the middle pull the couple far away, to the wonder beyond the sea. The Star at the centre says the main wonder is already here, and that neither of the two creates it alone.

sections.h2: Two weddings in one tale: the tail in the minus and in the plus
paragraphs: "Saltan" has two couples, and both marry by the same formula: "The tsar did not take long: he married that same evening" — "The prince did not take long, he married the princess." The son repeats his father's words but lives the tail differently. Two weddings — two ways to live 21-7-4.

paragraphs: A window frames the tale. It begins at a window: "Three maidens by the window were spinning late one evening" and dreamed of the whole world. Near the end there is a window again: "By the window Gvidon sits, silently gazing at the sea." The sea that "lashed" at the start now "does not roar, does not lash, only barely, barely trembles". And this time the prince does not fly to the world — the world comes to him: "Across the plains of the Ocean sails the fleet of Tsar Saltan." A couple that has built its kingdom stops chasing the world. The world sails in to visit.

The last thing Pushkin changed in the folk tale concerns The Emperor. In the 1824 note the ending is short: "and the stepmother dies". In Pushkin the three envious women hide in corners, are found, confess everything — and "the tsar, for such joy, let all three go home". A tsar who has seen the truth with his own eyes no longer needs an execution. Order rests not on fear but on joy.

sections.h2: What a 21-7-4 couple has to learn
paragraphs: Lisovskaya analyses a couple's tail this way: each conclusion carries, in brackets, the cards it follows from. Below are the tasks of a 21-7-4 couple taken apart the same way: from pairs of cards to the whole tail.

ul: **The World + The Emperor: rules agreed on, not rules inherited.** The freedom of The World and the order of The Emperor do not have to be at war. The task is to set shared rules together and revise them when life changes. A good test: can each of the two remember when and why a rule appeared, and do they agree with it today?

**The Chariot + The Emperor: decide important things with both present.** Saltan is wisest when he orders them "to wait for the tsar's return for a lawful decision". Nothing big about money, housing, children or family is decided by message, through go-betweens or in the other's absence. Waiting for the return is easier than fishing a barrel out of the sea later.

**The World + The Chariot: the road together, not apart.** A 21-7-4 couple comes alive in motion, but each may have their own road, and then home is only a change of trains. The task is to choose at least part of the way together: a city, a trip, a shared project. Gvidon flies after the ship alone while he is sad. Once married, he stays at home, and the motion comes to him by itself.

**The Emperor: say feelings out loud.** "With a sad thought on his face" is the portrait of someone who rules but does not say what is wrong. Among The Emperor's tasks Lisovskaya names exactly this: learning to talk about feelings. Four times the Swan opens a conversation with "What makes you sad?" — and it works better than any decree.

**The Chariot: restore strength rather than take it from those close.** After a business trip, a rush job or a move, The Chariot's tank is empty, and the easiest refuelling is at the partner's expense — irritation, demands, complaints. The task is to know in advance what restores each of the two, and not to mistake rest for winning an argument.

**The World + The Chariot + The Emperor: don't import the wonder from overseas.** As long as the couple measures its life by other people's tales of "such a wonder in the world", its own island will always seem too small. The task is to notice that the main thing in this union — The Star at the centre — is already there, and to build the kingdom around it, not around rumours.

paragraphs: If the "decree" in a couple rests on fear, threats or force, it is no longer a subject for reading the tail. Then a specialist is needed — a psychologist, and in danger, the local emergency number.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: "The couple's values" in the compatibility matrix answer what the union exists for. A 21-7-4 couple has only two options here.

83.8% of such couples have The Lovers. Waite calls it "the card of human love", and his divinatory list includes "trials overcome". For a 21-7-4 couple this fits the tale well: the union rests on a choice made with open eyes, after "think it all through well", and on the blessing "to live in counsel and love". The Lovers explain what the kingdom is built for: for the two, not for the throne.

16.2% of couples have The Devil in their values. For Lisovskaya it is a union of passion, a vivid bond and strong attachment, and even in the plus she warns that one partner may wake up wanting to possess the other. For such couples the Swan's words sound twice as loud: a wife is no mitten, and nor is a husband. The stronger the attachment, the more important it is not to confuse it with a right to keep someone tucked in a belt.

sections.h2: What Waite writes about The World, The Chariot and The Emperor
paragraphs: In the Major Arcana these three cards stand in the reverse order: The Emperor is fourth, The Chariot seventh, The World the last. The couple's tail runs against this current: from completion to foundation, from the whole world to a home of one's own. Waite describes The Chariot as "the victory which creates kingship as its natural consequence and not the vested royalty of the fourth card", that is, of The Emperor. In the 21-7-4 tail these two powers stand side by side: power won on the road, and power that has to be held at home.

On Waite's card The Emperor holds a sceptre and "a globe in his left hand". Wen explains: "The scepter or crux ansata is his sovereignty; the orb is his dominion." In Russian this orb is called derzhava, and the same word means a state, a power. Both senses come from the verb derzhat', "to hold". The World at the entry of the tail is the whole wide world, and in the main task it becomes an orb in the hand: something held. The couple's task is to hold their kingdom without crushing it in a fist.

On The World Waite sees a dancing figure in an oval garland and calls it an image "of joy attained in the body", "still guarded by the Divine Watchers". And on The Star, besides the woman with two ewers, there is "a shrub or tree, whereon a bird alights". Wen writes that "the bird perched on the tree conveys new opportunities that will restore hope". In Pushkin, hope also comes as a bird: "Look — over the flowing waters swims the white swan."

intro: The triple has an oddity that shows only in the numbers. The centre of the chart of every couple with the 21-7-4 tail is The Star, and no single person ever has The Star at the centre, whatever the date of birth. The brightest thing in this union belongs to neither of the two. Pushkin described such a couple long before any matrix: a prince is ready to walk after a bride with a star on her brow "even beyond thrice-nine lands", and the Swan answers him: "Why go far?"

ul: **M · Entry to the task — 21, The World.** The couple's common language is big plans: countries, moves, a life "for the whole world". The couple enters the union with this dream and stumbles over it too, because each has their own "whole world".

**N · Middle of the task — 7, The Chariot.** How the couple moves towards the task: in motion. Roads, projects, business trips, the chase after the next wonder — and decisions made on the move and at a distance.

**D · Main task — 4, The Emperor.** What the couple has to learn: to build their own kingdom — home, order, money, rules — without turning the partner into a subject. The key question of this tail is not "who is right" but "who decides, and how".

faq.q: Can 21-7-4 appear in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and 21 with a main task of 4 needs a centre of 17, which no person has. If 21, 7 and 4 stand in a row in a calculation, it is the karmic tail of a couple's matrix, that is, the compatibility of two people.

faq.q: What does "21-7-4 programme" mean in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: It is the same couple's karmic tail. Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the compatibility calculation follows, calls the triple on a couple's tail a "karmic programme". There is no separate entity behind the word "programme": these are the couple's tasks, read from the main point, The Emperor, through The Chariot and The World.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. The first number of a couple's tail is always divisible by three, so 4-7-21 and 7-21-4 are impossible, and the calculation never gives 21-4-7 for any dates. The 21-7-4 tail is one of a kind, and in every such couple it comes from the personal tails 18-3-12 and 3-22-19.

No. A couple's tail shows tasks, not a verdict or a forecast, and the method gives no compatibility percentages at all. By the method the main task of the tail is read mostly through the minus, because it is about what to learn. A 21-7-4 couple has The Star at the centre — an atmosphere of inspiration and mutual help that neither of the two has alone.

faq.q: Who is The Emperor in a 21-7-4 couple?
faq.a: Nobody by default, and not by sex. The Emperor here is the couple's task, not one partner's role. In different years and in different matters, first one and then the other turns out to be the "tsar". The task is to divide power into areas and decide important things together, by counsel rather than decree.

report: The brightest thing in a 21-7-4 couple belongs to neither of the two. At the centre of the chart of every such couple stands The Star, and no single person ever has this card at the centre of a personal matrix. It appears only between two people. Around it stand the three cards of the tail: The World at the entry, The Chariot in the middle, The Emperor as the main task. And behind them a story shows through, one that Pushkin finished in the summer of 1831, in the first year of his own marriage. A prince is ready to walk after a bride with a star on her brow "even beyond thrice-nine lands", and the Swan answers him: "Why go far?"

One sits silent and sad on a throne, the other rules by reports. The tale's own words divide it into two kingdoms. In the first half, "order", "letter" and "decree" rule, and all of it by messenger. At the end the same matters are settled by counsel: the young pair are blessed **"to live in counsel and love"**.

A squirrel with golden nuts can be put under guard, with "strict account" kept of her. When the prince asks for a third marvel, a wife, the Swan stops him for the first time: "But a wife is no mitten: you can't shake her off your white hand, nor tuck her into your belt." **A partner is not a mitten, not a treasury and not a subject.** In the tale, sex hands out the roles. In a 21-7-4 couple either of the two can be the tsar, the messenger or the Swan, and usually both take turns.

The Emperor grows up in a single line: "What am I — a tsar or a child? I'm going today!" In Waite's reversed list for The Emperor the last word is "immaturity". The child-tsar learns about the world from stories at court. The grown one boards a ship and sees for himself: "the tsar looks — and recognises".

report.h3: The Star is not imported from overseas

report: In the folk tale the star on the brow belonged to a child — the one born of two. Pushkin gave it to the bride. Four times the Swan asks the prince the same thing: "Why are you quiet as a rainy day? What makes you sad?" — and each time she helps. The Star at the centre of a couple works just like this: beside the partner, a person understands who they want to be. It has a minus too: love for a picture instead of a person. Gvidon falls in love with a rumour and doubts it himself: "But come — is it true?" And the answer comes from the one who has been beside him the whole tale: "Know that your fate is near: that princess is me."

A window frames the tale. At the start "three maidens by the window" dream of the whole world. Near the end "by the window Gvidon sits, silently gazing at the sea", and the sea "does not roar, does not lash". Once married, the prince no longer flies — and the world sails in to visit him with Tsar Saltan's fleet. The last thing Pushkin changed in the folk tale: there "the stepmother dies", while in his version "the tsar, for such joy, let all three go home". **Order rests not on fear but on joy.**
If the "decree" in a couple rests on fear, threats or force, it is no longer a subject for reading the tail: a psychologist is needed, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

unit.title: Counsel instead of decree

captions.M: To want the whole world for two and live by big plans
captions.N: To live on the road and not leave big things to go-betweens
captions.D: To rule together without making the partner a subject

unit.meaning: Your task is to decide big things together and face to face, by counsel, not by decree through go-betweens.
